The LORD says this (as in Samuel and Kings; 'The Lord GOD says this' for koh amar Adonai YHWH); note at first use in each book: the formula of a messenger delivering a king's words

the LORD declares (as in 2 Kings 19:33; 22:19), at the end of a clause, set off by commas; ne'um Adonai YHWH tseva'ot 'the Lord GOD of Armies declares'; note at first use in each book: ne'um is a noun, 'an utterance of the LORD'

oracle (as in Proverbs 30:1; 'The oracle concerning Babylon', Isaiah 13:1); note at first use in each book: from nasa' 'lift', so 'a lifting up (of the voice)'; KJV 'burden'; Jeremiah 23:33–40 plays on both senses

Woe to (before the people addressed, 'Woe to those who...'); in a funeral lament 'Alas' (1 Kings 13:30); a bare call to attention 'Hey!' or 'Come!' (Isaiah 55:1); note at first use in each book: hoy was the cry at a funeral
the day of the LORD / on that day
the Holy One of Israel (as in 2 Kings 19:22)
Daughter Zion / the virgin, Daughter Zion (as in 2 Kings 19:21 and Psalm 9:14); bat 'ammi 'my dear people' (literally 'the daughter of my people'), with a note at first use
young woman (as in Genesis 24:43; Exodus 2:8; Proverbs 30:19); at Isaiah 7:14 the note, the variant (Greek parthenos) and a traditions card give the 'virgin' reading and Matthew 1:23
my servant / the servant, lower case in the Plain (capitalizing would decide who he is); notes and the topic servant-of-the-lord give the readings

justice / righteousness ('justice and righteousness'); in Isaiah 40–66 tsedeq and tsedaqah often mean God's saving action, 'victory, rescue, vindication': by context, with a note at first use in each part
vision ('The vision of Isaiah son of Amoz', Isaiah 1:1); chazah 'see (in a vision)'
the Chaldeans (as in 2 Kings 25; note at first use in each book: the people of southern Babylonia, whose dynasty ruled Babylon from 626 BC; in Daniel also a class of learned men)
worthless idols (a play on 'elohim 'gods' and 'al 'not': 'nothings'); note at first use in each book

teaching, for the prophet's or the LORD's torah (Isaiah 1:10; 2:3; 5:24; 8:16, 20; 30:9; 42:4, 21, 24; 51:4, 7), as in Proverbs, with a note at 1:10 on the older 'law'; plural torot 'laws' (24:5). Why: in Isaiah torah is spoken instruction from a prophet or from God, parallel to 'the word of the LORD' (1:10; 2:3), and 2:3 plays on yarah 'teach'

the islands ('Islands, be silent before me!', Isaiah 41:1; 'The islands are waiting for his teaching', 42:4): the coastlands and islands of the Mediterranean, and so the far ends of the earth; singular 'i 'island, coast'. A gloss at first use in each part gives the sense 'far coastlands'
Ha! (a threat, where the LORD turns on his foes; hoy is not a lament or a call there; note at the verse)

turn (someone's) fortunes around ('I will turn Moab's fortunes around', 48:47), as in Job 42:10; note at first use in each part: literally 'turn back the turning' or 'bring back the captivity' (KJV, and Deuteronomy 30:3 on this site); the phrase plays on shuv 'turn', Jeremiah's key verb, and means a full reversal, not only a return from exile
Terror all around (as in Psalm 31:13 on this site; Pashhur's new name in 20:3 'Terror All Around'); note at first use in each part: Jeremiah's catchphrase, which his enemies threw back at him (20:10)
